items.text: USTR announced affirmative findings in 14 of its 16 Section 301 'structural excess capacity' investigations and proposed new tariffs on those economies. Proposed top rates: China up to 20% (10% for some goods, alternative up to 40%), the EU, Japan, South Korea, Switzerland and Taiwan up to 15%, Singapore 20%, India 25% (17% with a trade deal), Vietnam 35% (20% with a deal), and Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand, Cambodia and Bangladesh up to 18%. For the 13 non-China economies, goods already under Section 232 tariffs (steel, aluminium, copper, vehicles, chips, patented drugs and more) are excluded. No determinations were made yet for Mexico and Norway. Comments are due Jan 5, 2027 and hearings start Jan 25, 2027 at the USITC, so no tariffs take effect before early 2027, after the US-China truce expires Jan 10. On Nov 26, India's commerce ministry said it has no structural overcapacity in any sector, the European Commission rejected the idea that Europe is a source of overcapacity, and China's foreign ministry said the problem does not really exist.
items.notes: Earlier WSJ/Bloomberg reports said 16 economies; the actual announcement covers 14 (Mexico, Norway pending). Foreign reactions come from Nation Press (IANS) summary. Law-firm alerts (Wiley, Baker McKenzie) used for terms; USTR's own notice not fetched.

items.text: The PCE price index, the Fed's preferred inflation gauge, rose 3.8% year on year in October, up from 3.6% and in line with forecasts. Core PCE rose 3.3%, above the 3.2% expected and the fastest since late 2023, with both measures up 0.3% on the month. Personal income jumped 0.7%, partly on one-off Medicare premium rebates, while inflation-adjusted spending was flat. The same morning, third-quarter GDP growth was revised up to 4.3% annualised from 3.4%, led by investment and consumer spending. The Fed's Beige Book said activity grew in eight of 12 districts and prices kept rising moderately. CME FedWatch put the odds of a quarter-point hike on Dec 9 at about 98%.
items.notes: Sources differ on September headline PCE (3.6% per Stock Analysis, 3.7% per Capp Notes). BEA release not fetched directly.

items.text: Stocks had a volatile pre-holiday session. The Nasdaq fell as much as 4.6% intraday in an AI-led sell-off before closing down 0.62% at 23,585.80. The S&P 500 ended down 0.25% at 7,182.78, and the Dow erased a loss of more than 1,100 points to close up 0.33% at 50,182.95. Nvidia fell about 3.9% (down about 27% in November), with Micron and Oracle also lower amid worries about AI costs and debt, and S&P Global put Nvidia's AA credit rating on CreditWatch Negative, citing governance risk. Brent rose 3.5% to $94.61 after Yemen's Houthis claimed a strike on Saudi Arabia's Ras Tanura refinery. Markets were closed for Thanksgiving on Nov 26 and close early on Nov 27.

Treasury's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) said it is investigating a cybersecurity incident involving unauthorised access to a limited subset of its systems and took some systems offline as a precaution. The Bank Secrecy Act e-filing site, used by banks to report suspicious activity, stayed up, though some services were unavailable. FinCEN extended deadlines for eligible filings due Nov 18 to Dec 29 to Dec 30. A FinCEN official said Treasury is working with the FBI, CISA and outside forensic examiners. The Register found no sign so far of access to BSA or beneficial-ownership data. It is the latest in a run of federal incidents, including the FBI NCIC breach and a USDA breach.

Hackers breached an unclassified system that the CIA and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence use for open-source intelligence analysis, CNN reported citing four sources, after The New York Times first reported the intrusion. A Defense Department agency, which one source identified as the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency, was also reportedly affected. An ODNI official said there was no disruption to critical capabilities or classified systems; the CIA declined to comment. Early indications point to an origin in China, though it is unclear whether the Chinese government was involved, and investigators suspect use of an open-source AI hacking tool the FBI warned about this month. Two sources said it does not appear linked to the FBI NCIC breach; any link to the FinCEN incident is unclear.
items.reporter: Sean Lyngaas, Kristen Holmes, Katie Bo Lillis
items.notes: NYT first reported on Nov 24 (US time); CNN follow-up Nov 25. Attribution to China is preliminary and anonymous.

items.text: The White House announced a 'whole-of-government' push to protect critical infrastructure from cyberattacks as federal breaches pile up. The release lists Kirsten Davies' nomination as National Cyber Director and Gen. Joshua Rudd at the head of NSA and Cyber Command, and says cyber policy teams are being reorganised under the National Security and Homeland Security Councils. Agencies must patch high-risk vulnerabilities within three days. CISA has launched a 'CI Fortify' programme for operators and will add more than 400 staff, and the FCC has barred new foreign-made consumer routers judged a security risk. A DOJ-FBI cyber-defence initiative is due next week. The release does not name a new executive order.
items.notes: Official account only; it largely gathers earlier actions together. The three-day patch mandate may come from an earlier directive.

items.text: Vice President JD Vance told reporters in Ohio that Justice Department and national-security officials assured him Jensen Huang was not under investigation. Vance reportedly passed that assurance to Nvidia's board before it reinstated Huang on Nov 23. Reports the same day said DOJ had not opened an investigation into Huang before Trump pushed for his return. AG Todd Blanche earlier said inquiries into Huang were not necessarily a formal investigation, while DOJ and Commerce continue to probe Singapore-based Megaspeed, which was added to a trade-restriction list on Nov 23, over chips allegedly diverted to China. Huang sits for a closed House interview on Dec 1 and a public Senate Banking hearing on Dec 3.
items.notes: CNN and CNBC pages could not be fetched; details come from Wise Voter's summary and TechCrunch (Tim Fernholz). Critics say the assurance came from political officials, not a closed investigation.

items.text: Judge Christopher Cooper of the federal district court in D.C. issued a preliminary injunction blocking Trump's second birthright-citizenship executive order, signed in August, and certified a class of plaintiffs. The order would have denied citizenship to US-born children of parents working for foreign governments or international organisations without diplomatic immunity, children born through commercial surrogacy, and children of suspected gang members or terrorists. Cooper wrote that the Citizenship Clause promises citizenship to practically all children born in the US, and that the president cannot create new exceptions. Reports describe him as the second judge to block the order. DOJ and the White House did not immediately comment.
items.notes: Washington Times and AP headlines call this the second judge to block the order; the first ruling was not verified here.

items.text: The CDC raised its count of measles-related deaths in 2026 to nine, Reuters reported, although state figures add up to at least 14 (nine in Pennsylvania, three in Wisconsin, one each in Virginia and New York). Confirmed cases reached 6,039 across 47 jurisdictions as of Nov 24, with 671 hospitalisations and 43 outbreaks this year. An HHS spokesperson said the tally rose after the National Center for Health Statistics verified more state death reports. The gap comes from the CDC's switch under Secretary Kennedy to NCHS mortality data instead of state counts.

The DEA proposed mid-year increases to its 2026 production quotas for several controlled substances (Docket DEA-1568A), published in the Federal Register on Nov 25. ADHD stimulant ceilings would rise sharply: d-amphetamine about 40%, mixed amphetamine about 31%, lisdexamfetamine about 23% and methylphenidate about 19%. Quotas for research psychedelics such as psilocybin (+20%) also rise, while fentanyl is essentially unchanged. Comments are due Dec 28, 2026.
items.notes: Figures come from the CASRAI summary of FR doc 2026-23959; the FR text itself was not fetched.

items.text: Trump told the New York Post that the Iran campaign is funded through the end of January and questioned how Democrats could politically justify cutting it off, while acknowledging that his options may narrow once Democrats control Congress. He said Israel's goal of regime change in Iran was 'probably doable' but not his own aim, which is preventing an Iranian nuclear weapon. The IRGC claimed two more tankers exploded in the Strait of Hormuz early on Nov 25, blaming mines after the ships took a 'false route'; this is not independently verified. No Iranian tanker convoy or US interception was reported.
items.notes: The Trump remarks come from the NY Post interview as reported by The National; IRGC tanker claims are unverified.

items.text: Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan conceded the Alaska Senate race to Democrat Mary Peltola, saying Alaskans deserve confidence in their elections and that he expects the ongoing investigations to answer remaining questions. His concession effectively ends talk of a recount (deadline Nov 28) or a state election contest. Federal and state probes continue into allegations that Peltola's campaign helped recruit a second 'Dan Sullivan' onto the ballot, which her campaign denies; the administration had earlier dropped its suit to block certification. Republican senators who floated refusing to seat her have not recently pressed the idea.
items.notes: The concession was on Nov 24 but was not logged in the previous brief.

items.text: Trump issued the annual Thanksgiving Day proclamation, declaring Nov 26 a national day of thanksgiving and tying it to America's 250th-anniversary year. Media reports say he is spending the holiday in Florida. It was the only presidential action posted for Nov 24-26 apart from the Nov 23 death-penalty memorandum.

In a video posted on Wednesday evening, Prime Minister Donald Tusk urged President Karol Nawrocki to sign the PIT/CIT amendment passed by the Sejm on Nov 5 and the Senate on Nov 6. The law raises the first PIT threshold from 120,000 to 130,000 zł, adds a 24% band for income of 130,000–150,000 zł, and lifts CIT to 22% for firms with revenue above €50m. Tusk said about 3.5 million taxpayers (some 5 million people) would benefit, that he had heard the President was hesitating, and that Nawrocki has already vetoed 50 laws in 16 months, a record he warned him not to extend. As of Wednesday night no decision had been announced; Infor puts the constitutional deadline at Nov 27. No statement from the President's Chancellery was reported in the coverage.
items.notes: Pro-government framing from Tusk; no Chancellery response found. Do not confuse with the separate tax-relief act signed earlier (E-261125-26).

items.text: The Council of Ministers adopted a resolution, published in Monitor Polski and in force on adoption, saying the Constitutional Tribunal's work is seriously threatened because the National Bank of Poland has halted all payment orders from the Tribunal's accounts since Nov 16. It tasks the Prime Minister and the Finance and Economy Minister with steps to protect the State Treasury's interests, citing risks of unpaid obligations and compensation claims. The NBP froze the accounts citing doubts over who legally represents the Tribunal amid the dispute between Bogdan Święczkowski and the judges' majority led by Anna Korwin-Piotrowska. NBP had asked both sides to bring a court action by Nov 27; Korwin-Piotrowska rejected that route and demanded the legal basis within three business days, while Święczkowski's lawyer demanded the underlying documents. Justice Minister Żurek blamed an unnamed NBP figure and said a 'plan B' for funding exists.
items.notes: Coverage found is from centrist/liberal outlets (Prawo.pl, RMF24/PAP, Polsat); no right-leaning reaction to the resolution found. Earlier, right-leaning nczas.info framed the NBP freeze neutrally as Glapiński halting payments.

items.text: Prosecutor General Waldemar Żurek said Tribunal judge Anna Korwin-Piotrowska had handed him four General Assembly resolutions consenting to prosecution: three for Bogdan Święczkowski (blocking judges from ruling and violating Judge Maciej Berek's bodily integrity; unlawfully delegating nine prosecutors; exceeding powers over operational monitoring concerning Roman Giertych) and one for Vice-President Bartłomiej Sochański. Two further motions against Święczkowski failed on formal defects. Żurek said prosecutors may now charge and question Święczkowski as a suspect; no charges were confirmed. The same day Święczkowski spoke at the European Parliament in Strasbourg, and Żurek said the ECHR had unanimously rejected his request for an interim measure to keep exercising his functions. Warsaw mayor Rafał Trzaskowski also refused to extend a protest assembly outside the Tribunal building.
items.notes: Account of the resolutions is from Żurek (X post and interview). Święczkowski's side calls the assembly and suspension unlawful; his EP remarks were reported under a headline about an 'organised criminal group' but not detailed.

items.text: Senate Marshal Małgorzata Kidawa-Błońska confirmed the Senate received two nominations for the Monetary Policy Council by the Nov 25 deadline: economist Prof. Marcin Piątkowski (Kozminski University, ex-World Bank/IMF), put forward by the Left, and KO MP and former health minister Izabela Leszczyna, put forward by Civic Coalition. No other candidates were reported. Budget committee chair Kazimierz Kleina said the committee would consider them within two weeks, and a Senate vote could come at the Dec 16–18 sitting. They would replace Ludwik Kotecki and Przemysław Litwiniuk, who moved to the NBP board; the seats must be filled within three months of the Nov 6 recall.
items.notes: Dziennik.pl highlighted that Leszczyna has no economics degree; critics on the right question a politician's appointment to the RPP.

items.text: GUS preliminary Labour Force Survey (BAEL) data show unemployment at 3.5% in Q3 2026, up from 3.2% in Q2 and 3.1% a year earlier. The activity rate rose to 59.0% from 58.7% and the employment rate to 56.9% from 56.8%. Registered unemployment for October stayed at 5.8%, with 905,300 registered jobless, up 38,000 (4.4%) year on year, while job vacancies fell to 34,900. Bank Pocztowy's Agata Łysakowska attributed the year-on-year rise to cautious hiring amid rising labour costs and expects registered unemployment of about 5.9% by year-end.
items.notes: Spidersweb headline called it the highest BAEL unemployment since the pandemic.

items.text: Deputy Defence Minister Cezary Tomczyk said Poland needs a small no-fly zone along the eastern border, a few to around a dozen kilometres deep, and expects the regulation to take effect in late December or early January. He said that about two months ago Polish pilots switched from visual to 'positive' identification, and that the zone would add a further criterion: an aircraft entering it from Ukraine and confirmed on radar would be grounds for shooting it down. The move follows the Nov 20 incursion of three Russian Kh-101 cruise missiles that fell in Lubelskie and Podkarpackie.
items.thread: Russian missiles and drones over Poland

items.text: Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski told Polish Radio's Trójka that shooting down Russian missiles or drones over Ukraine, at Kyiv's request, would fall within necessary defence, since objects heading for Polish airspace are already a direct threat. He said the question needs detailed discussion with Polish military experts and NATO headquarters. On the summoned Russian ambassador Georgy Mikhno, he said expulsion is an option but Poland will not pursue it yet, as Russia would retaliate. The ministry said Mikhno received a very sharp protest note; he denied any Russian link.
items.thread: Russian missiles and drones over Poland
items.notes: A GSC disinformation report (Nov 25) says officials indicated NATO does not favour shooting down missiles over Ukraine; no decision taken.

items.text: Chełm mayor Jakub Banaszek called for direct talks between the government and border-city mayors on security after the missile and drone incidents, saying eastern Poland faces its deepest economic crisis and asking that Finance Minister Domański join any meeting with Tusk and Kosiniak-Kamysz. Defence Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz replied that he was already in talks with eastern municipalities and had spoken to the mayor. He said an order to shoot down intruding objects was issued on Friday, with the final decision left to the pilot, and that the government spends 5–6bn zł a year on shelters and storage.
items.thread: Russian missiles and drones over Poland

items.text: Russian businessmen Sergei Kolesnikov and Igor Rybakov, co-owners of the Technonicol group, are suing Poland, Bank Polski, Holcim AG, Holcim Polska and a former court administrator in the Moscow arbitration court for over 462m zł (9.2bn roubles) plus interest. The claim concerns the mineral-wool plant in Wykroty (Lower Silesia), placed under forced administration after Russia's invasion of Ukraine and taken over by Holcim Polska; the founders are on Poland's sanctions list. The court postponed the merits hearing to April 15 because foreign defendants had not been properly notified.
items.notes: Article gives the hearing day as 'Wednesday (24 November)'; Nov 24 was a Tuesday, so the exact hearing date is uncertain.

items.text: At about 17:10 on Wednesday a man set himself on fire in front of the Ministry of Culture, opposite the Presidential Palace in Warsaw, State Protection Service spokesman Col. Bogusław Piórkowski confirmed. SOP officers and passers-by helped him first; he was taken to hospital and, according to a later GSC risk report, to intensive care. Police cordoned off the area and a prosecutor is investigating. No motive has been given.

The Regional Court in Katowice rejected appeals against the 88-day pre-trial detention of MP Wojciech Król, suspended from the Civic Coalition club and chair of the National Media Council, making the Nov 5 order final. He faces four corruption-related charges brought by the European Public Prosecutor's Office over tram modernisation contracts in the Upper Silesian-Zagłębie Metropolis, including alleged benefits such as a trip to Thailand and use of a villa worth 3.8m zł. He denies the charges.

The Energy Minister's notice set maximum pump prices for Thursday Nov 26 at 5.82 zł/l for Pb95 (from 5.84), 6.48 zł/l for Pb98 (from 6.51) and 7.15 zł/l for diesel (from 7.23). All three caps fell again, with diesel down 8 grosze. The next notice, for Friday, is due on Thursday.

Prime Minister Tusk arrived in Brussels for the extraordinary European Council on the 2028–2034 budget and Ukraine's 2027 financing, which opened Thursday with a euro-summit session and is due to end Friday. António Costa's Nov 21 negotiating box is €204bn smaller than the Commission's proposal, with cuts to cohesion and competitiveness. Poland's main objection is the plan to send ETS auction revenue to the EU budget; Costa proposes phasing it in from 0% in 2028 to 30% by 2034, which PiS MEP Bogdan Rzońca called a way to mask Poland's eventual losses. Tusk has said he will not accept a budget that raises energy prices or weakens eastern-flank defence. Germany's Merz wants Ukraine aid linked to the budget, and the Netherlands wants a smaller budget or bigger rebate. No outcome was available at time of writing.
items.notes: Arrival confirmed only via PAP-based Portal Samorządowy headline (page did not load). Opposition (PiS) argues the ETS phase-in is a trap; government presents its red lines as defending Poland.

items.text: At the extraordinary City Council session on 25 Nov, called by KO and Nowa Lewica, Mayor Łukasz Gibała kept the halt on metro preparations. He said work will resume only if the government guarantees funding through one of three routes: a special metro act, money in the state budget, or a city–government financing agreement. The metro stays in city strategy documents as a conditional investment. The city's metro tenders are suspended, including the design-documentation tender, which several outlets value at about 40m zł. Deputy Mayor Karol Wałachowski presented the spending analysis: about 4.5m zł spent directly from January 2025 to October 2026, of which about 2.3m zł was staff costs and 1.11m zł advisory contracts. The figure excludes other city units. PiS MP Andrzej Adamczyk said his party will table a 30m zł amendment to the 2027 state budget for concept and geological work. KO MP Dominik Jaśkowiec urged the mayor to be bold and pointed to EU, defence and BGK money, and KO senator Monika Piątkowska called dropping the project irresponsible. No resolutions on the metro were voted.
items.notes: Outlets disagree on the 40m zł figure. KRKnews (Armada) says about 40m zł was spent on documentation. Puls Krakowa and Kurier Krakowski say 40m zł was the planned or estimated value of the documentation tender, and Puls gives 4.5m zł actually spent. The planned-tender reading looks right. Polsat News (25 Nov) quotes Gibała as saying the metro office cost nearly 5m zł over two years. None of the sources mention the geological-survey tender or the KIO appeal. No source reported the outcome of the Music Centre resolution (second item on the agenda).

items.text: An order signed by Mayor Łukasz Gibała lets businesses on Rynek Główny that hold temporary land-use agreements with the city suspend, cancel or get back fees for the period after the 7 Nov attack when restrictions stopped them working. It covers restaurant gardens, horse-carriage operators, itinerant traders, and artistic and advertising activity. 7 and 8 Nov are included automatically. Firms can apply for further days, up to 9 Dec at the latest, with a statement explaining why they could not operate. Applications go to City Hall's Administrative Affairs Department by 30 Nov, one per business. In justified cases the department head may also end the agreement. This is separate from the ZBK rent cut for tenants of municipal premises.
items.notes: Radio Kraków published it early on 26 Nov from a PAP report. Several outlets (ESKA, SE, Portal Samorządowy) carried the same story.

items.text: The Electoral College of the University of the National Education Commission (UKEN) in Kraków removed rector Prof. Piotr Borek from office by secret ballot: 102 for, 40 against and 2 abstentions out of 144 voters. The resolution took effect immediately. Science Minister Marcin Kulasek filed the motion on 30 Sep, citing breaches of labour law and union rights shown in final labour-court rulings on staff dismissals. An earlier direct dismissal by the ministry had been overturned on 29 Sep by the Warsaw administrative court, which found the statutory grounds were not proven. That ruling is not final. The minister then suspended Borek and asked the electors to act. Coverage did not say who runs the university now or when a new rector will be elected.
items.notes: Borek is widely described as close to PiS. OKO.press (liberal) frames him as having broken the law under PiS protection. Right-leaning coverage of this vote was not read.

items.text: Tatra National Park (TPN) rejected Tatra county's plan to run horse carts on the full route to Morskie Oko from 1 December. TPN says the shortened route (Palenica Białczańska–Wodogrzmoty Mickiewicza, about 3 km) is how the 2025 letter of intent is meant to work, and that carriage operators turned down its proposed winter conditions. From 1 Dec TPN will stop organising winter transport and close its parking areas to carriage operators. Any county-run service would go ahead without TPN's consent and, it warns, would raise road-safety risks. The climate ministry gave no direct comment and referred media to TPN's position. The carriage operators' association led by Andrzej Mąka backs the county head.
items.notes: rp.pl and Gazeta Krakowska covered the same dispute; neither page was read in full. The ministry has not commented directly.

items.text: Election officials finished checking the petition for a referendum to recall Limanowa's mayor, Jolanta Juszkiewicz, and the town council, and found enough valid signatures: 1,123 of nearly 1,800 submitted. Organisers accuse the authorities of straining finances, stalling investments, controversial staffing changes, removing a Pietà image from the town banner and demolishing the railway station. The mayor and councillors reject the accusations. The district election commissioner will set the date, possibly in late January. It is the third recall referendum in the Limanowa area this term.
items.notes: Małopolska region story, not Kraków city.

items.text: A Supreme Court bench of CJI Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V. Mohana issued notice to the Delhi Police on fresh bail pleas from Umar Khalid and Sharjeel Imam in the 2020 Delhi riots 'larger conspiracy' UAPA case. It declined to take up interim bail that day, saying the police should respond first. The bench sent the matter to the CJI on the administrative side so that a three-judge bench can be formed, because a May 22 reference order (Tasleem Ahmed) flagged a conflict between the Gulfisha Fatima ruling and the 2021 K.A. Najeeb judgment, which the CJI himself wrote. He remarked that he felt a little embarrassed that two benches had read his judgment differently. Kapil Sibal (for Khalid) and Siddharth Dave (for Imam) stressed that both men have been jailed for more than six years and that no witness has yet been examined. No next date was reported.
items.notes: The LiveLaw report (https://www.livelaw.in/top-stories/supreme-court-issues-notice-to-delhi-police-on-umar-khalid-sharjeel-imam-bail-pleas-refuses-to-consider-interim-bail-today-559880) was seen in search results only. Neither report mentions submissions by the Delhi Police or ASG.

items.text: The Union Cabinet approved an ₹11,000 crore scheme to build a domestic manufacturing base for construction and infrastructure equipment (CIE), run by the Ministry of Heavy Industries. Eligible original equipment and component makers will get sales-linked incentives of 8–13% of incremental sales over five years, 2028-29 to 2032-33, after a two-year gestation period. Covered equipment includes tunnel boring machines, hydraulic excavators, ship-to-shore cranes and off-highway trucks. Up to ₹375 crore in viability gap funding goes to a national CIE testing facility. PM Modi called it a big push to make India a global hub for such equipment. Piyush Goyal tied it to China's export restrictions on tunnel boring machines, in force since Nov 18.
items.notes: BS sidebar links suggest other recent cabinet approvals (India Post schemes ₹2,632 cr, Kamarajar port terminal ₹4,288 cr), but their dates were not verified, so they are not logged.

items.text: Indian equities rebounded sharply when trading resumed after the Guru Nanak Jayanti holiday. The Sensex rose 1,502 points (1.82%) to 83,938.28 and the Nifty 50 rose 470 points (1.85%) to 25,819.25, recovering Monday's fall. Private banks and financials led, and FMCG rose 3.79% with Hindustan Unilever up about 5.5%. Metals (-2.04%) and media (-4.44%) lagged. Brokers credited continued foreign institutional buying and softer crude, with Brent around $88. Marketcalls reports the rupee hit a seven-month high intraday, at about 92.2 per dollar. Trading ended before the USTR tariff proposal was published.
items.notes: The rupee figure is from Marketcalls and is not an official RBI reference rate. Business Recorder headline: Indian stocks close to wiping out their 2026 losses as foreign money returns.

items.text: On the first day of a two-day special session, the Jharkhand Assembly passed a resolution by voice vote opposing the Election Commission's Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls and seeking its immediate halt. The resolution asks the Centre for a new SOP drawn up with political parties. Minister Radhakrishna Kishore, who moved it, said 27% of the state's 2.21 crore voters had been marked suspicious and sent notices. He called the EC the Centre's puppet and urged that CEC Gyanesh Kumar be removed, though that demand is not in the resolution text. Leader of Opposition Babulal Marandi (BJP) called the session politically motivated. He said 43 lakh names were deleted, including 7.63 lakh dead voters, 15.53 lakh who had moved, 4.38 lakh duplicates and 14.50 lakh untraceable. BJP MLA Champai Soren defended the SIR as a way to remove illegal voters.
items.thread: Opposition vs Election Commission over SIR
items.notes: Ruling JMM–Congress–RJD: the SIR disenfranchises voters. BJP: it cleans the rolls of dead, shifted and illegal voters. The IANS headline says the resolution seeks the CEC's removal, but PTI says that demand was recorded only as a minister's statement.

items.text: MeitY Secretary S. Krishnan said the government does not see Sarvam AI's hosting of Chinese open-weight models as violating the IndiaAI Mission's principles or misusing state incentives. Sarvam, one of the first startups picked under the ₹10,372 crore mission to build a sovereign model, drew criticism this month for its new 'Token Factory' platform. The platform sells access to models including DeepSeek, GLM and Kimi alongside Google's Gemma. Krishnan said AI firms need ways to earn revenue and that the government itself uses some of these services. He described building an indigenous frontier model as separate from Sarvam's model-access business.
items.notes: Critics argue that a state-backed 'sovereign AI' firm should not resell Chinese models; Bloomberg also covered the backlash (seen via aggregators).

items.text: Speaking at the launch of Chariot-1, MeitY Secretary S. Krishnan said the government's AI regulation consultation papers are in their final stages and will be released shortly. He gave no date or details of their content. Chariot-1 is a family of audio-native foundation models from Chariot Artificial Intelligence (formerly Gan.ai), one of the first four teams chosen under the IndiaAI Mission to build sovereign foundation models. It supports English and 10 Indian languages and combines text generation, text-to-speech and speech recognition in one architecture. The developers say a shared script representation cuts the tokens needed for Indian-language text by about 2.5 times.
items.notes: In October MediaNama reported MeitY would publish an AI regulation consultation paper within a month, so the release is running late.

items.text: At the MEA's weekly briefing, spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said India has held several engagements with Russia in recent weeks on bilateral, multilateral and regional issues and ongoing conflicts. He cited External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar's Monday (Nov 23) phone call with Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov. Moscow said the call covered the bilateral agenda and current international issues, and Jaishankar described it as a discussion of recent developments. It followed a Nov 9 call that focused on Ukraine. Separately, Jaishankar briefed visiting defence journalists from about 30 countries in New Delhi on Nov 25.
items.notes: The call itself took place on Nov 23, outside the window; only the MEA's Nov 25 comments are new.

items.text: India is marking Constitution Day (Samvidhan Divas) on Nov 26, the 77th anniversary of the Constituent Assembly's adoption of the Constitution in 1949. The Ministry of Parliamentary Affairs is coordinating an online Preamble reading on MyGov in 23 languages and a Constitution quiz on MyGov and MyBharat (Nov 18–26). Viksit Bharat Yuva Samvad events are running in 786 districts across all 36 states and UTs from Nov 24 to 26. Ministries, states and schools are holding seminars, debates and special assemblies. No official theme was announced, and reports of the main leaders' events had not appeared by the time of writing.
items.notes: A DD India sidebar mentions PM Modi paying homage to Ambedkar on Constitution Day; the text was not seen.

items.text: Nov 26 marks 18 years since the 2008 Mumbai terror attacks, with tributes at Mumbai Police headquarters, CSMT, Cama Hospital and the Tukaram Omble memorial at Girgaon Chowpatty. Business Standard's anniversary piece says Tahawwur Rana, extradited from the US in April 2025, is still in Tihar Jail awaiting the framing of charges, while Abu Jundal's trial continues. Proclamation orders against six other accused, including Hafiz Saeed and Zaki-ur-Rehman Lakhvi, have not been executed.
items.notes: Anniversary item; no new legal development in the window.
